about:
At 16, Augustine Pasin left his family and home in Chicago to pursue Chinese studies. He enrolled as the first Western student at a Shanghai boarding school where he helped his Chinese classmates write a school constitution, create the school’s first student council, and propose the “student voice” position to which he was later elected. He combined his passion for service and foreign cultures by co-founding an organization that tutors local Chinese university students in English. Augustine was named valedictorian of his graduating class. 

In 2017, Augustine was accepted and named a Hesburgh-Yusko scholar by the University of Notre Dame, At Notre Dame, Augustine aimed to improve cross-cultural and economic relations between the United States and China. Augustine also studied study German in Berlin and served as a philosophy research assistant at Heidelberg University. He graduated with a major in China Studies, a minor in Business-Economics, a 3.9 GPA, and Latin Honors. 

After graduating, Augustine was accepted into the prestigious Yenching Academy Masters of China Studies at Peking University in Beijing. There he explored the export of Chinese internet literature.

Augustine graduated Magna Cum Laude from Notre Dame's Mendoza College of Business with Master of Science in Finance. 

He currently works at PwC as an associate in the Cloud & Digital SAP Finance practice. 

Augustine has a passion for foreign languages and cultures that drives him to move to and explore international cities. He has lived and studied in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Chicago, New York, Boston, Berlin, Vienna, and Heidelberg. He hopes to explore even more cities in the future.

featured.subtitle: Augustine Pasin - MsF (Fin), MA (Econ History), BA (Chinese) on LinkedIn

slides.title: Imposter Syndrome: The Struggle to Internalize Success
slides.subtitle: Augustine Pasin - MsF (Fin), MA (Econ History), BA (Chinese) on LinkedIn
slides.description: Part 1 – of our Leadership Transition Series An Introduction: To begin this article, we’d like to reference an anecdote from famed author Neil Gaiman and his own experiences with imposter syndrome. On his blog, he writes: To preface this article, we have to make a clear distinction between Imposter Syndrome and feelings of Imposterism. Although leadership language and articles often refer to ‘Imposter Syndrome’, this language is not precisely correct. What is often referred to as Imposter Syndrome is instead Feelings of Imposterism (FOI). Let us be clear: Imposter Syndrome is a serious, psychological condition that is best handled by professional psychologists. Those with Imposter Syndrome suffer through chronic feelings of intellectual fraudulence that override any feelings of success or external proof of confidence (Gill Corkindale, 2008). It is also by no means uncommon, especially among the academic and business elite. It is estimated that between 25-30% of high-achieving individuals may suffer from Imposter Syndrome. If, after reading this article, you believe you might be suffering from Imposter Syndrome and not feelings of Imposterism – please seek professional help. In a milder form, Feelings of Imposterism (FOI) on the other hand are much more common. A study conducted in 2011 found that almost 70% of all adults experience feelings of Imposterism at some point during their life (Sakulku & Alexander, 2011). So, it should not come as a surprise that many of our clients at MagnoliaTree – all of whom are senior executives and decision-makers of strategy – suffer from this struggle to internalize success. What is surprising, is how few of our clients know about FOI, its effects, and how to overcome it. This piece will focus heavily on the latter condition: temporary FOI associated with taking on new roles, transitioning to a new company, or during a period of crisis. As many of us have struggled with radically new working conditions in the wake of a COVID-19 workforce, it is likely that you have faced feelings of Imposterism. Through our research and experience, we hope to provide those struggling with Imposterism a clearer picture of the condition that is Imposter Syndrome and methods of dealing with these feelings of inadequacy. This article is the result of significant research into the condition and the psychological research which has been conducted on it. However, it is by no means a definitive piece on the topic. Should you want to learn more about Imposter Syndrome or Imposterism please utilize the resources provided at the bottom of this piece. With that, let us explore Imposter Syndrome and feelings of Imposterism. So, What Is Imposter Syndrome? The first research paper on the Imposter Syndrome was written by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes about 35 years ago. They sought to explain why high-achieving women were struggling to internalize their success and labelled their feelings of fraudulence in the face of achievement Imposter Phenomenon. The pair noted that imposters, “see themselves as unworthy of the level of praise they are receiving because they do not believe they have earned such recognition based on their capabilities, causing heightened levels of anxiety and stress.” (Clance & Imes, 1985) While many of the initial studies into imposter syndrome examined primarily women, contemporary research has revealed that imposter syndrome affects men and women equally and is likely associated with perfectionism. Recent studies suggest that between 25-30% of high achievers may suffer from imposter syndrome and around 70% of adults may experience Imposterism at least once in their lifetime. (Sakulku & Alexander, 2011) That is to say, FOI is by no means rare, and you should not feel alone or isolated by the experience. With a basic understanding of what imposter syndrome is, let’s examine a list of the ways in which Imposterism can present itself in the workplace and beyond: FOI is especially prevalent as we take on new roles or challenges. This is especially true during the current global pandemic, where many of us have had to transition into radically new work structures. In the words of Kets de Vries (2005), “To some extent, of course, we are all imposters. We play roles on the stage of life, presenting a public self that differs from the private self we share with intimates and morphing both selves as circumstances demand. Displaying a façade is part and parcel of the human condition.” Imposterism is a natural part of life and it should be treated as such. The feelings of inadequacy we face in new roles, or facing new challenges, can be overwhelming but are also often temporary. Fortunately, there are many proven methods of dealing with Imposterism revealed by psychologists and experienced professionals exploring Imposter Syndrome. The unintended consequence of Imposter Syndrome and Imposterism: The psychological consequences of Imposter Syndrome can be severe. Although Imposter Syndrome is not an official psychological diagnosis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), it is often associated with anxiety, depression, and perfectionism. Both Imposter Syndrome and Imposterism can also have significant motivational and performance consequences in the workplace. FOI sufferers internalize failure a lot more than positive feedback. They undervalue wins while overvaluing failures. FOI can lead to a vicious cycle of perfectionism, wherein the subject strives for perfection and as a result drags out deadlines. These delays raise concerns amongst leadership, which is then internalized by the sufferer finds themself facing greater self-doubt which in turn fuels even higher levels of perfectionism leading to a downward spiral. As mentioned above, FOI often rears its head during times of transition. It is particularly important to watch out for two radically different, but nonetheless dangerous outlets for FOI when transitioning to a new position or company. Firstly, FOI can result in stagnant growth. When arriving at a new career, someone suffering from FOI may find themselves less likely to take risks or experiment for fear of failure, thus leading to stagnation. Those transitioning into leadership positions are especially susceptible. These people will likely default to their comfort zones. For example, a first-time manager might reflexively focus on producing content rather than leading. It’s important to remember that “what got you here, won’t get you there.” On the flip side, an individual with FOI in the midst of a major transition might instead find themselves jumping to rash decisions in order to prove their worth. Especially during the first 1-2 weeks at a new position, they might attempt to make all of the decisions by themselves, in the process ignoring the opinions of peers, mentors, and subordinates. This can be a dangerous foundation for a new career that WILL NOT lead to followership. How to deal with Feelings of Imposterism: Here is a compiled list of methods by which you can resolve FOI: The first step, and perhaps most important, is to recognize that you are experiencing imposter feelings. From there onward, you can consider how to deal with these feelings. Seek support. Needing help is natural, everything doesn’t have to be done alone. A coach and a mentor are great pathfinders in helping you navigate through these emotions. A simple step to alleviating feelings of Imposterism is to talk. Seek out your coach, mentors, friends, and family and explain the situation. Often, getting the issue off your chest can help take off some of the anxiety and pressure you are experiencing. The next step is to contextualize the imposter feelings you are facing, ideally together with a trusted advisor. Have you experienced a new challenge, and new career, or some other shift that is causing these feelings of Imposterism? What is the source of these feelings? Feeling useless right now is not the same as being useless. If the source of your Imposterism is a failure, reframe your experience as a learning opportunity. Be kind to yourself. Mistakes are normal, especially in a new and challenging environment. Use your failures as a chance to grow. Lastly, seek ongoing feedback and support. Don’t attempt to do everything by yourself, especially in a new position. This will only result in feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope with the situation, which can intensify the feeling of being an ‘imposter’. For people leaders in the workplace, here are additional opportunities to institute organization-wide programs to deal with FOI: Consider instituting a program to help others deal with their own feelings of Imposterism. Both California Technology and MIT have instituted programs to debunk myths about belonging and help students to identify Imposter Syndrome tendencies. Many universities include counseling workshops to help students identify their strengths, deal with failures, and understand perfectionism to set more reasonable expectations for themselves (Cokely, 2013). Consider doing the same in your office. Huffstutler and Varnell (2004) also encourage the development of peer group programs, mentoring opportunities, and identification of organizational expectations, especially those that produce high levels of anxiety. They also recommend instituting a system of mentors to help new employees and long-term employees alike adapt to new challenges. Other recommendations have included the implementation of multifaceted structured feedback systems (Cogner & Fulmer, 2004), If you have experienced Imposterism or Imposter Syndrome, we would appreciate you sharing any resources or advice that you may have regarding the condition. Below is a list of further resources on Imposter Syndrome, Imposterism, and how to deal with both. Know that if you are facing feelings of inadequacy, you are not alone. Further resources: Books: Beating the Imposter Syndrome by Portia R. Mount The Empress Has No Clothes by Joyce Roché The Secret Thoughts of Successful Women by Valerie Young Articles/Papers: The Imposter Phenomenon in Higher Education: Incidence and Impact, Anna Parkman, Ohio Dominican University Overcoming Imposter Syndrome, Gill Carindale How to Succeed When You Have Big Shoes to Fill, Rebecca Zucker Podcasts: The Imposter Syndrome Files Imposter Syndrome

slides.title: Living in a Copy: Thames Town
slides.subtitle: Augustine Pasin - MsF (Fin), MA (Econ History), BA (Chinese) on LinkedIn
slides.description: For three years, I lived in a ghost town in the Songjiang District of Shanghai modelled after Victorian England called Thames Town. Now for the segue. Here are the three things Thames Town taught me about leadership. 1. Never fake something Thames Town is a ghost town for a reason. It is virtually uninhabitable. What might first appear as authentic recreations of Victorian town-homes are, in fact, shallow facades built with cheap mortar, concrete and paint. The few buildings are functioning are home to British staples such as McDonalds, a Familymart (a Japanese chain of mini-marts), and a very out-of-place Baskin-Robbins (a classic American ice-cream shop now owned by Dunkin' Donuts). Many leaders have built similar facades, hiding their personality behind a recreation of perceived leadership qualities. They are who they think they HAVE TO be. But much like the copied Thames Town, we can see through the illusion quickly. Whenever you fake something, it comes with a huge price tag on your own mental health and leads to a distrusting and disengaged workforce. Rather than pretending to be something you are not (and spend 5 billion yuan in the process), play to your strengths. 2. There is a difference between borrowing and copying Thames Town is a shameless attempt to attract domestic tourism by copying classic British architectural styling, and some part of me respects the architects for their brazenness, but Thames Town is the living embodiment of copying off of your classmate’s exam. Then somehow still failing the exam. There is nothing wrong with borrowing ideas, styling, or structure from those who have found success in their art. However, rarely does the exact same formula work twice (with the exception perhaps of pop music). When creating a business, a work of art, or an academic essay, it is important to adapt your strategy to fit your own goals, your audience, and whatever relevant variables apply to your format. No one can implement your ideas in the way you can! It is the uniqueness of one’s leadership that is inspiring to others. Adopt models, surveys, leadership styles but make them YOUR OWN. 3. Seeing past the superficial Here is the twist. Yes, our collective middle-school teachers had a point. There is intrinsic value in creating something of quality that one's peers notice and value. And the antithesis of the saying is on full display with Thames Town However, I cannot discredit the end product. Everyday hundreds of Shanghainese couples visit Thames Town to have their pictures taken next to the congregation-less Church, or to smile next to the Queen's Guards or statues of famous historical British icons like Harry Potter (pictured on the right). In the end, Thames Town succeeded in its goal of attracting domestic tourism and is a beloved weekend hot-spot for Shanghai natives, despite its tackiness and poor execution. So, in spite of its flaws, Thames Town is a statement to understanding your audience. It is a reminder to me that even low-quality products, with proper execution and consumer awareness, can flourish. And that even if something is superficially unappealing, it is important to empathize with those that enjoy it in order to better understand one's audience. I believe this can apply to leaders as well. It is highly probable that your budgets will be cut, that you will be faced with less funds available to invest in talent than you would like. Still, there is much you can do on a low budget that will create joy, a positive vibe and reinforce the right behaviors. How about hand-written “thank you” cards? Pizza deliveries on Friday? Or virtual coffee sessions? Even when the tools you have are limited make the best out of it. Even when you admire the people around you, get inspired. But don’t copy. Borrow, adjust and own it! All Facades begin to crumble eventually and that’s okay. All that matters is that there is something behind that facade. Despite its garish appearance; shoddy craftsmanship; and absence of authentic British brands, I always enjoyed hanging out around Thames Town with my friends on the weekend. Grabbing an ice-cream from Baskin-Robbins. Or practicing my Chinese with the lovely elderly woman behind the counter at Familymart. So, my final piece of leadership advice is to see beyond the superficial. You might find a diamond hidden within the coal.

headline: Principal at PwC

location.linkedinText: Washington, District of Columbia, United States

experience.description:
Marco Fiaccadori is a principal in the transfer pricing practice of PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP’s Washington National Tax Services.  

Marco is an economist specializing in supporting multinational companies with their international tax strategies and assisting clients with all aspects of transfer pricing - including tax planning and implementation, tax compliance, and tax controversy and dispute resolution, including advance pricing agreements and Competent Authority matters. 

In his role of senior economist of the PwC transfer pricing practice Marco works on clients across the national network with a particular emphasis supporting technical needs of clients receiving services from the APMA and TP Tax Controversy practice and providing deep technical knowledge to address complex matters around intellectual property valuation, intercompany transfers of risk and evolving views around value chain profit attribution.  He serves as technical resource to the TP practice markets, particularly in the Washington metro area and Philadelphia, supporting engagement teams in audit disputes and developing scalable solutions for complex economic issues related to transfer pricing.  Marco is a senior level economic and technical resource for the PwC's National Economics Team (NET) within the TP practice to develop market solutions and train staff.  

His clients range from large global companies to mid-sized privately held companies, and span most industries from chemicals and pharmaceuticals and life sciences to consumer products, technology and retail. 

Marco is a frequent invited speaker at conferences and has been publishing widely on technical tax and transfer pricing valuation matters.  He holds a B.A. (summa cum laude) from Bocconi University and an M.A. and a Ph.D. in economics from the University of Chicago where he was a lecturer in economics at the College.

headline: Culture | Leadership | Transformation
about:
I am passionate about generating impact on every project I undertake and working with people that dream of changing the world in their own way. I am an avid learner of the psychology behind people's actions, which drives my curiosity towards learning more about incentives, organizational structures, behavioral economics, and irrational behavior. 

From my 3 years working at Tecnológico de Monterrey, I became proficient in translating high-level ideas into concrete products and implementing them. This required understanding both senior managers' visions and end users' requirements. I am looking for opportunities to engage with people and organizations that are mission-driven, boast an entrepreneurial mindset, and rely on powerful values to drive their actions.

These four tenets are my mantra: 

1) Define my purpose in life and strive for it
2) Work hard and don't complain or preach about it
3) Find the beauty within the people
4) Plan only the necessary, enjoy the journey!

These four principles steer my everyday actions, driving both my professional and personal attitude towards work and personal endeavors.

headline: US Tax Partner at PwC.   Former leader of PwC’s US Tax practice with unique insights across tax policy, planning and reporting.
about:
Ken Kuykendall is a partner at PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), where he is the US tax leader, tax consulting leader, and a member of the US Leadership Team for the firm. Ken’s passion is collaborating to solve business problems for clients, and he teams with a national network of over 50,000 tax, consulting and audit professionals every day to deliver quality and differentiated, tech-enabled outcomes for US and multinational clients. Ken works closely with the rest of the PwC US leadership team to develop and drive firm strategy and coordinate with the PwC global network of firms to deliver an unparalleled client experience to the US and global marketplace. 

Ken brings to his roles a deep knowledge of the US tax system, decades of experience advising clients across a number of industries, and extensive relationships in industry and government. He has over 30 years of experience working with multinational corporations on a broad spectrum of tax and business issues. He has advised a variety of governmental and administrative agencies including the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), the Internal Revenue Service, the US Congress and the US Treasury on tax and financial reporting matters.
 
Previously, Ken served the US firm as Tax Managing Partner, the Tax Services and National Tax Services Leader, as well as the Leader of the Risk & Regulatory Platform. Ken has also served as Director of Taxation for a Fortune 500 company and has first-hand experience with strategically managing the day-to-day aspects of a US tax function.
 
Ken has a B.A. in accounting from Eastern Illinois University, a M.S. in taxation from DePaul University, and a J.D. from The John Marshall Law School in Chicago. He is a member of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants and the American Bar Association.

slides.title: She cried..
slides.subtitle: Samkelo Mtshali on LinkedIn
slides.description: At 23:28 I write, after a long day of mixed emotions I finally have time to myself to reflect. I watched the countdown...30..29...28..27..26..25.....5..4..3..2..1...0, I looked at my phone, total silence. My heart sank! I got a call, ignored it for a sec then answered.."Congratulation.." my heart jumped. A notification came through...'Dear Samkelo, Congratulations SAICA would like to confirm that.." I stopped. I got my APC results!! It was not just results, it was the sweat, the long hours, the hidden tears, the silent battles that were fought, it was those mornings that I felt like not getting up, it was the tough times of not doing what you want to because you have a dream, it was the tough moments of discipline, the late nights and the mostly it was the sacrifices that were made! They finally paid off. I stopped . I shed a tear! Colleagues came running in the office, I hid that tear, I saw the excitement in their eyes, the happiness, in that moment I felt life as it should be. I got up, still shaking in disbelief, who am I to be in such a position? Who am I to attain this? I found myself walking into the boardroom, I was met by a round of applause. I was still shaking, I was not there mentally. I was crying internally. I got that letter then walked out. I am not sure where I was. I remembered almost quitting this journey in 2016, I remember almost giving up. I was back at that point, Lord, am I glad that I did not quit! This is it, this is the moment I have been waiting for, the moment I persevered for. I am just an ordinary guy, nothing special at all but at this moment..you see this moment! Man! I got back to the boardroom where I was waiting for the results, with a dry mouth i uttered "when You show up Lord, You show off!" then a tear ran down. I got back to my senses, I remembered I had a phone....0..8..3..9..9....it starts to ring,"Yes Samke"..."Thobe I just passed my board exam"......"I am driving I cannot scream!! This is great news, but I knew you were going to make it, how did Lungi do?" I hung up, it starts to sink in now, I am here and this is me, me! I called mummy this time, before she said hello, I broke down and said "mum I made it, your son has completed the board exams" She cried, it was not just a cry, it was a cry of relief, a cry that all those prayers have been answered, it was the cry of a mother who witnessed her son struggle right up until now, it was a cry for all those silent times where I saw that she'd like to spend time with me but I just had so much, it was a cry of a woman who had to pick me up when I was at my lowest, she broke down in a way that built me, after that cry she uttered "My womb has produced a CA(SA)" this coming from a woman with no fancy background yet gave me the best life a kid could ask for. She uttered " My son is a CA(SA)" that moment I was in total silent, that was a moment to life. The day then proceeded, congratulations were pouring in, compliments and heartfelt messages. It is amazing how many people look up to an ordinary person and looking back I am happy that I did not quit because I did not know that the kid that was going through what I went through was looking at me as an inspiration. Above all of this though.. ...My mum she cried, this was definitely for her.

headline: Lead Tax Partner
about:
A conceptual thinker, Bret sees patterns and opportunities where others see complexity. As a lead tax partner with 25 years of public accounting experience, he provides his clients with a broad perspective on tax and business issues, along with strong tax technical and accounting skills. Bret has led engagements relating tax provision preparation and assurance review, M&A issues, structural planning, state and local issues, tax compliance, tax controversies, and cross border tax planning. 

Passionate about creating wins for his clients, Bret has developed long standing and meaningful connections with the Technology, Consumer Markets, and Private Equity Sectors. Clients describe his open, approachable style of communication as energizing and fun. He saves his highly competitive side for dealing with tax examinations and controversies.

Over his career, Bret has worked in PwC's federal industry tax practice, the mergers and acqusitions group, and the state and local tax group. He has written on a broad range of tax topics, including contributions to CCH's California Tax Analysis, Aspen Law & Business' Tax Considerations of Construction Litigation, and the PwC Global Tax Summary - United States Chapter.

Away from work, Bret spends most of his time with his wife and three children. His passion for cooking brings the family together, and their shared love of hiking helps offset the impacts of their culinary tastes.

A native of Chicago, Bret has a B.A. from the University of Illinois – Champaign/Urbana, and a J.D./L.L.M Taxation from the University of San Diego School of Law.

He can be reached at bret.h.balonick@pwc.com, and at PwC’s San Francisco office (415) 498-5000.

Common misspelling: Brett, Brad, Brent, Balonik, Balanick, Balanik

Keywords: corporate, international, state, planning, compliance, controversy, structuring, restructuring, provision, return, consulting, assurance

experience.description:
As a Lead Tax Partner, Bret is the first point of contact for his clients in addressing crucial and complex tax issues.  In this role, Bret relies on comprehensive network of tax specialists, both in the US and abroad.  In addition to delivering PwC's network of tax specialists, Bret has significant experience in the following functional areas:

INCOME TAX ACCOUNTING - Bret currently serves as the lead tax partner on several SEC registrant assurance clients, responsible for auditing the accuracy and reasonableness of the registrant's provision for income taxes.  Separately, Bret is also responsible for the preparation of income tax accruals for several public and private companies.

TAX COMPLIANCE -   Bret leads several compliance engagements for a broad range of clients, from mulitinational SEC registrants to emerging clients.  In this capacity, Bret is responsible for federal, state, and global income tax compliance for his clients.

MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS - Bret has significant experience with respect to buy and sell side due diligence, subchapter C issues, and analysis and planning regarding corporate distributions and redemptions. projects.title: Google Data Analytics Case Study
projects.description:
As an enthusiastic cyclist and a frequent NYC Citi Bike rider, I analyzed Divvy's Chicago bike share data for my Google Data Analytics case study. The goal is to reveal member and non-member customers' riding patterns and make strategies to convert casual riders into annual members.

First, I used Google's BigQuery to clean the data, including removing rows lacking data and adding calculated fields needed for further analysis. Next, I used R to get a statistical summary of the cleaned data and generate bar charts to compare member rides and casual rides in different contexts. I documented my code using R Markdown and Kaggle Notebook. Last, I used Tableau to create a Chicago city map visualizing the geographic distribution of the bike stations that member and casual riders most frequently started and ended at to show how they use the bikes differently. These steps effectively helped me understand the profiles of the two groups of shared bike users and make recommendations to help the business grow.

projects.title: Inventory Management System Using Image Processing
projects.associatedWith: Associated with The D J Sanghvi College of Engineering, Mumbai
projects.description: Our project dealt with the sorting of hardware pieces (nuts, bolts, and screws) based on their type and size. A conveyor belt mechanism was used to get the pieces under a camera, which sent the video stream to MATLAB. A microcontroller Arduino interfaced with the laptop was responsible for controlling a servo motor, which had a turntable with boxes for the different types of pieces. Our image processing code in MATLAB identified the type of piece, and prompted the Arduino to rotate the servo motor to the angle at which the box of that particular type of hardware was located, thereby accomplishing the sorting process.

headline: Senior Manager - Workday Practice | Workday Learning & Talent expert
about:
Workday Architect | Certified in HCM, Learning, Talent, PEX, Recruiting | 25+ Years in ERP & HCM Transformation

With over 25 years of experience across ERP and HRIS/HCM transformation programs, I bring a deep understanding of complex IT landscapes across diverse industries and domains. Since joining the Workday ecosystem in 2018, I’ve discovered my professional ikigai—a true alignment of purpose and passion. Workday isn’t just my job—it’s my craft.

As a certified Workday professional in Core HCM, Learning Management, Talent & Performance, People Experience (PEX), Recruiting, Engagement Management (EM), and Medium Enterprise, I’ve led and contributed to 30+ successful Workday implementations, including global rollouts of Workday Learning and Talent for large and mid-sized enterprises.

My approach is hands-on, research-driven, and constantly evolving. I push myself to stay ahead—supporting clients, mentoring peers, and contributing to the broader Workday Community.

Having journeyed through various technologies, roles, and industries—often before roadmaps existed—I view my broad experience as a strategic advantage. It equips me to adapt, lead, and deliver in any environment.

Outside of work, I’m a passionate home décor enthusiast, self-taught artist, part-time blogger, and an unapologetic bibliophile. And if you're up for a game of Scrabble, be warned—I play to win!

Let’s connect to share insights, discuss ideas, or explore collaboration in the Workday space.

I’m currently completing my Bachelor’s degree in Accounting and Risk Management & Insurance at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, with graduation scheduled for December 2025.  Following that, I’m excited to begin my professional journey full-time with PwC in Chicago, as a part of the Real Estate - Tax team.

My academic background combines a strong technical foundation in accounting principles with a strategic understanding of enterprise risk—equipping me to bring value in both financial accuracy and business risk insight.  During my college career, I’ve engaged in hands-on experiences that deepened my knowledge in:
Financial reporting & analysis
Audit and assurance
Corporate risk management
Insurance and regulatory frameworks

I’m especially drawn to the intersection of accounting and risk—where analytical rigor meets strategic decision-making. Whether it’s identifying financial discrepancies or evaluating operational exposures, I thrive on helping organizations see the full picture.

What drives me:
Asking better questions to uncover smarter solutions
Working collaboratively to deliver real business impact
Building a career grounded in integrity, client service, and continuous learning

I'm eager to start my journey with PwC, where I’ll be surrounded by forward-thinking professionals and contribute to solving complex problems for clients across industries.

headline: Manager - PwC Legal Business Solutions
about:
As a regulatory and commercial legal advisor with 7+ years of experience, I specialize in helping companies navigate complex legal landscapes—particularly at the intersection of innovation, compliance, and business operations. My career has spanned Fortune 500 companies, top-tier consultancies, and in-house legal departments, where I’ve led initiatives in antitrust compliance, M&A integration, contract negotiation, and legal transformation.

Currently, I serve as a Manager in PwC’s Legal Business Solutions practice, where I lead regulatory compliance initiatives and develop operational playbooks that improve efficiency and reduce legal risk for clients across sectors. I’ve also managed cross-border M&A legal workstreams and built compliance frameworks aligned with U.S. and EU regulations, including the Digital Markets Act and GDPR.

Previously, I was a Regulatory Affairs Senior Specialist at Discover, leading responses to federal and state regulators, streamlining internal processes, and supporting enterprise-level exam readiness and remediation planning.

From conducting complex legal analysis to designing training programs that foster a culture of compliance, I bring a business-minded, solutions-oriented approach to every challenge. Whether supporting capital projects, designing policy frameworks, or managing outside counsel, I thrive in fast-paced, highly regulated environments.

I’m passionate about leveraging my legal expertise to support growth, manage risk, and contribute to mission-driven innovation.

experience.description:
Chris is leading PwC's US Global Trade Services team as National Leader. With over 25 years of experience, Chris specializes in guiding clients through the complexities of the global trade landscape, including tariffs, duty drawback, and First Sale for Export, all while considering the interplay of transfer pricing, international tax, and global supply chain matters.

Chris excels in developing customized trade, transfer pricing, and value chain strategies that empower clients to navigate global challenges confidently. His approach integrates in-depth policy analysis with cutting-edge technology and modeling, ensuring businesses can optimize their operations effectively. Through meticulous project management and a commitment to responsiveness, Chris ensures that clients receive the highest standard of service.

MemoryWeb is an upstart / bootstrapped family photo app that was developed based upon three founder's personal needs that were not being solved. We solve the problem where you can have all your photos in one place, automatically uploaded, tagged and ready to explore. Moreover, you photos can be linked via file DNA to your ancestors so your present and past photos are connected. 

MemoryWeb is like a personal assistant for people who have no time to organize all their photos. We do the heavy lifting, automatically finding and tagging entire collections, so people can sit back and enjoy their photos immediately and explore them in ways never seen before. We also preserve the context behind each photo forever and if they want, people can share these socially, individually, and fully bundled with all details directly to another MemoryWeb account. 

Our motto “for you, for them, forever” was fueled by the need for immediate enjoyment and long-term preservation that was not delivered by any one solution. Until now.

Leaving the safety net of a fast-tracking career with international accounting firms, Christopher took a huge personal gamble by starting his own company.  Armed with ideas and ambition for building a better mousetrap, Christopher was shocked to learn that how easily he fell into the rut of business as usual. publications.title: Amid trade turmoil, manufacturers may be leaving money on the table
publications.description:
Trade is a top concern for global business executives this year, according to PwC’s 22nd Annual CEO Survey. Trade conflicts and protectionism were both among the top 10 threats to growth cited by respondents, and given the seemingly endless parade of headlines about tariffs and currency manipulation, it’s easy to see why. With Washington and Beijing locked in conflict, perhaps U.S. businesses can be forgiven if they feel at the mercy of forces beyond their control.

But there is one underappreciated tool that companies can leverage to help manage their exposure to tariffs. They could be eligible to recover significant amounts of money they paid to the U.S. government in the form of customs duties, taxes and fees under a mechanism called duty drawback. Nearly as old as the United States itself, it offers the opportunity to secure a refund of 99% of the duties, taxes and fees paid on goods imported into the U.S. that are subsequently exported to a third country, or destroyed. Recent changes to U.S. trade law make it an even more attractive tool.

headline:
Pragmatic Technologist | Next-Gen Tech Navigator | Human-Centered Innovation | IP Informed | 
Proud Father | Maker of Things
about:
I like tech! That is the core of who I am and the passion that drives my development. Ever since I can remember, I have been fixated on destroying and repairing gadgets, working on computers, playing video games, and messing with anything that went "beep" or "boop." I was lucky enough that when I was in high school, I had access to a premier computer lab way beyond anything else in the Chicago-land area. It was there I was finally able to turn my "hobby" into a skill. 

I turned my interest into a computer engineering degree and that into a law degree where I prosecuted patents for tech companies and research institutes. I gained of lot of knowledge in those years, about how business works and how to understand a truly inventive approach versus a derivative idea. It's these experiences that have provided me the tools to view the world in a different way.

Fast forward to today and I lead PwC's Emerging Technology Research team where it's my job to not only understand technology but to see how these technologies converge with one another. I help companies understand where technology is going and when it is right to make a move. I do not pretend that I can predict the future, but my knowledge, background, and understanding of tech uniquely qualifies me to stitch together ideas and experiences using emerging technology that are not readily apparent to others. I understand user experience, infrastructure, and the components needed to make that happen.

Above all, I'm a tech guy. I get up in the morning and I read blogs, aggregators, articles about tech when others are watching the morning news. It's the DNA of who I am. It's sort of cool!

experience.description: Frequent speaker both internally and externally on the topic of emerging technologies. Subject matter specialist on numerous different emerging technology domains including metaverse, web3, extended reality, etc.

I lead PwC's Emerging Technology Research team. Our team is focused on providing emerging technology research to support our internal and external teams. We are also responsible for providing materials to train and upskill members of the firm. This can range from providing one-page in depth dossiers on technologies such as AI, AR, VR, 3DP or any number of other emerging techs, to in depth playbooks detailing the implementation of such technologies. We also provide live training both internally to the firm as well as externally.

I have trained over 2,000 people on the essential emerging technologies. I was also involved in the intial discovery and development of PwC's Essential Eight emerging technologies which is core to our ET identity. We are focused on delivering the right information that is relevant, but also including a unique lens of a technologist providing insights that only an expert can bring.

Finally, we maintain our internal platform that is used to assess which emerging technologies are a focus area for our clients. My team maintains technology information and industry/business trends that enable PwC to perform a technology assessment to focus client's efforts on the most impactful emerging technologies.

publications.title: The Study of User Experience Within Advertising in Virtual Reality
publications.publishedAt: HCI in Business, Government and Organizations · Jul 17, 2023
publications.description: The growing adoption of virtual reality (VR) introduces marketing campaigns that are unlike traditional advertising techniques. The immersion of VR technology allows advertisers to create simulated interactions for products with a more significant impact than two-dimensional (2D) alternatives. Participants in this study underwent a series of games, embedded with advertisements, to better understand user sentiment between static and immersive advertisements. User surveys spatial data and time-based data show that users prefer and engage more with immersive advertisements rather than 2D banners which are more commonly represented in Web 2.0 environments. Gamifying brand interactions and rewarding user engagement yielded positive user feedback. In addition, this paper highlights key concerns around data security and privacy users may have with advertising marketing agencies should consider. This study outlines potential key mechanisms in driving experiential marketing tactics for virtual environments and increasing advertisement conversions.

publications.title: Taming the Code: Effectively Implimenting Software Patents
publications.publishedAt: The John Marshall Review of Intellectual Property Law · Jan 1, 2006
publications.description: Software patents are a sore subject for many programmers. Although still in their infancy, they have managed to anger many of those in the programming community. Software patents started to evolve in the early 80’s through multiple court decisions that eventually defined software as statutory patentable material. Although patentable, software has proven to be a formidable match for the examination process. The examination process has proven ineffective in properly examining software patent applications and as result multiple lawsuits based on frivolous patents have emerged. Potential battles such as the one between Creative and Apple over Creative’s patent for a hierarchal file system have become examples for which opponents of software patents can rely. This comment proposes the creation of a third party entity that would be made up of the programming community that would police software patent applications prior to issuance. This entity would alleviate the strain on the USPTO as well as examiners while rebuilding the reputation of software patents and the USPTO.

publications.title: Social Vulnerability and COVID-19: Changes in Trauma Activations at a Safety-Net Hospital
publications.description: Following the declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic, there were reports of decreased trauma hospitalizations, although violent crime persisted. COVID-19 has had the greatest impact on minoritized and vulnerable communities. Decreases in traumatic events may not extend to these communities, given pandemic-related socioeconomic and psychological burdens that increase the risk of exposure to trauma and violence.

publications.title: Social Vulnerability and Appendicitis: Single-Institution Study in a High Insurance State
publications.description: Multiple factors signifying higher social vulnerability, including lower socioeconomic status and minority race, have been associated with presentation with complicated appendicitis (CA). In this study, we compared the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of our population by appendicitis severity (uncomplicated appendicitis [UA] versus CA). We hypothesized that SVI would be similar between patients with UA and CA presenting to our institution, a safety-net hospital in a state with high healthcare insurance coverage.

publications.title: The utility of perforated appendix rate as a proxy for timely access to care
The Geographic Association between Incidence of Acute Appendicitis and Socioeconomic Status – A Population-based Analysis
publications.description: Numerous studies have found that socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with risk of perforated appendicitis (PA) among patients with acute appendicitis (AA). A potential limitation is their use of proportions of PA among AA, which assumes that incidence of AA is evenly distributed across populations at risk. This study examines spatial heterogeneities in the incidence of AA/PA and hypothesizes that variations in incidence of both are associated with SES.

Training: In the training module we are experimenting with different approaches to assist individuals with learning discrete areas of the law more quickly.

Research:  In the research module we are experimenting with different approaches to enable individuals to more efficiently research specific legal issues.

Practice: In the practice module we are experimenting with tools that will either make the practice of law more efficient or reduce error.  

At present, the site is solely limited to U.S. federal income tax topics.

honorsAndAwards.description: Edmund J. James Scholar programs are named for the fourth president of the University of Illinois, Edmund J. James. Since the 1950s, the University of Illinois has encouraged outstanding undergraduate students by offering participation in the Edmund James Scholar Program. Each college has a James Scholar Program undergraduate honors program. The James Scholar program recognizes the top 10% of students as measured by academic achievement.  Students are invited to join the James Scholar program based upon their application for admission to the college as an incoming freshman. Any student who was not admitted to the college as a James Scholar and completes the first year in the top 10% of the class will receive an invitation to join the program.
